CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the 5–10% retaliation already in force on ~$60B of U.S. goods and open a channel for talks that seek a pause or cancellation of the scheduled January 1, 2019 jump of List 3 from 10% to 25% — without new purchase quotas, MIC 2025 rollback, or unilateral tariff cuts. Do not add another tariff tranche or a demonstrative yuan break through 7. Further tariff escalation would hand Washington a pretext for the threatened ~$267B residual list; premature purchase concessions would repeat the May “trade war on hold” episode, when a goods-buy offer was pocketed and Section 301 still proceeded.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. As of 24 September the United States has 25% on ~$50B plus 10% on ~$200B of Chinese goods (~$250B combined 301 coverage), explicitly aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and Made in China 2025, with the 10% rate set to become 25% on 1 January 2019. That is a material hit to the export model and to tech-upgrading goals, and the April ZTE denial order showed a single U.S. entity action can halt a national champion. FX pressure is already visible: CNY weakened from ~6.28 in early April to 6.876 on 26 September (~9.5%), a move that only partly offsets 10% duties and that the PBOC has begun to lean against (counter-cyclical factor, defense of 7). Reserves are still ~$3.11T (down ~1.2% in the window), industrial production is still expanding at 5.8% y/y (down from 7.0% in April), and seasonally adjusted merchandise exports rose into September — so the real economy has not cracked and this is not an existential/financial-stability event. Action should therefore stay near zero. China has already used most remaining U.S. import ammunition (2017 U.S. goods imports ~$154B; $50B matched at 25% plus $60B at 5–10%). A further tariff hike would be asymmetric and could trigger List 4 covering nearly all remaining Chinese shipments to the United States. The May 19 joint statement (“significantly increase” purchases; Mnuchin “on hold”) collapsed ten days later when the White House proceeded with the $50B 301 plan, so conceding purchases or structural reform now, with no locked U.S. tariff standstill, would buy nothing. Negotiate: keep current counter-duties, invite pragmatic dialogue aimed at freezing the January rate hike, and reserve non-tariff tools rather than spend the last tariff chips.
key_factors: List 3 (10% on ~$200B) took effect 24 Sep 2018; combined U.S. 301 coverage now ~$250B and is scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 Jan 2019
Trump has already threatened a residual ~$267B list if China keeps retaliating — covering nearly all remaining Chinese exports to the U.S.
China just imposed 5–10% on ~$60B and is short of U.S. goods that can be taxed without self-harm
CNY −9.5% vs USD since April; PBOC defending ~7; reserves still ~$3.11T
China IP still +5.8% y/y and merchandise exports still rising — tariffs have not yet broken the real economy
May purchase truce collapsed when the U.S. proceeded with 301; do not concede purchases without a tariff freeze
ZTE denial order (Apr–Jul) showed firm-level U.S. kill-switch risk; Huawei/ZTE U.S. government-use ban signed in August

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China total reserves ex-gold ~$3.106T on 2018-09-01, down ~1.2% over the window — still a large buffer.
China industrial production still expanding: 105.8 in Sep 2018 vs 107.0 in Apr (y/y index), a slowdown not a contraction.
China merchandise exports SA still rising into Sep 2018 ($216.3B vs $208.6B in April).
If China does retaliate, the Administration “will immediately pursue phase three, which is tariffs on approximately $267 billion of additional imports.”
China announced a tariff hike on $60B of U.S. products; appealed for “pragmatic dialogue”; AmCham warned of a downward spiral and 52% of surveyed firms reported slower customs clearance.
PBOC reintroduced a counter-cyclical factor on Aug 24 after the yuan approached 6.93; officials have vowed not to use depreciation as a trade-war weapon.
